properties.decision:
RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. Alex's idea, 2026-08-14 (docs/feedback/2026-08-14-alex-grok-session.md, Opportunities), in his words: "`record_change` should refuse (or warn) if the target's current hash already differs from what the caller thinks they are snapshotting — or be a required first step inside the typed merge when `status` is `accepted`."

DELIBERATELY SEPARATE FROM `fact:defect-record-change-overwrites-the-name-of-the-event-it-is-filed-under`, which the near-duplicate guard surfaced: BOTH ARE FAILURES OF THE SAME CALL AND THEY ARE NOT THE SAME FAILURE. That fact is about `record_change` clobbering the ChangeEvent's `name`, found serially; this is about the SNAPSHOT capturing state that had already moved, found under parallel writes. Whether they get one fix is part of what is open here — which is an argument for keeping them separate until somebody decides, not for merging them now.

WHAT HE HIT (his item 2): in one batch he `record_change`d a Decision AFTER a sibling `add_decision` on the same id had already merged. The Snapshot stored the NEW statement. Nothing warned. In his words: "the timeline for that revision is a lie; easy for any agent that parallelizes writes."

THE OPTIONS:

(a) REFUSE ON A HASH MISMATCH — the caller states what it believes it is snapshotting; a difference is refused. CHEAP, and it matches doctrine already applied elsewhere: `set_artifact_checksum` is a two-sided accept for this reason, and `export_graph` refuses a divergent write rather than silently discarding. COUNTER: the caller has no hash in hand today, so this needs a new argument, and an agent that cannot produce one gets a tool it cannot call.

(b) WARN RATHER THAN REFUSE. CHEAP, breaks nothing. COUNTER: the loss is silent precisely because the call reports success, and a warning nobody reads is this project's own recurring failure.

(c) FOLD IT INTO THE TYPED MERGE when `status` is `accepted` — his stronger form: you cannot edit an accepted Decision without the snapshot happening first, because the tool does it. STRONGEST; removes the ordering hazard rather than reporting it. COUNTER: it makes one write path do two things, and `dec:ask-not-repair` is the standing preference for naming a problem over acting on it.

(d) DO NOTHING; THE DISCIPLINE IS THE ANSWER. COUNTER, and it is measured rather than argued: the sibling fact was found on 2026-08-15 doing exactly this, STRICTLY SERIALLY and in the order `revise-design` prescribes, and data was lost anyway. Ordering discipline is demonstrably not sufficient for this call — which is evidence against (d) rather than for any particular replacement.

NOT ESTABLISHED: how often the parallel-write case actually occurs — one report, one session.
properties.name: IDEA — the record-before-you-edit discipline can silently snapshot the NEW state. Should `record_change` refuse when the target has already moved, or be folded into the typed merge itself?
properties.rationale:
Recorded via the brainstorm skill at `proposed`, options with counters beside them, nothing promoted. Kept distinct from the name-overwrite fact after the guard named it: two failures of one call, found by two different routes, and whether one fix covers both is itself part of the open question.

⭐ UPDATED 2026-08-16 — A FIFTH OPTION ARRIVED BY SHIPPING SOMETHING ELSE, and it weakens (a), (b) and (c) without settling them. v0.32.0 gave every typed constructor a `revision` block: landing on an existing node now returns the properties the call OVERWROTE, with their prior values IN FULL, plus a `changed` flag and a `prior_content_hash`. Its own note names this exact ordering — snapshot BEFORE the merge, because afterwards it files the replacement as the prior state.

⇒ (e) THE INFORMATION IS NOW IN THE REPLY, SO PERHAPS NOTHING MORE IS OWED. A caller who merges first and snapshots second is now TOLD, in the merge's own response, what the prior value was — which is the fact the lying Snapshot destroyed, handed back at the moment of destruction. COUNTER, and it is why this does not close the question: the block reports to whoever reads the reply, and the failure mode here is an agent parallelising writes and reading nothing. A value returned to a caller who does not look is not the same as a refusal. ⇒ The open question narrows usefully: it is no longer 'how do we preserve the prior value' but 'does a returned value suffice, or must the ordering be enforced'.

📌 AND THE PRIOR-HASH OBJECTION TO (a) IS NOW WEAKER TOO: the counter said a caller has no hash in hand, so refusing on a mismatch needs a new argument. `prior_content_hash` is now returned by the constructors, so a caller who has touched the node HAS one.
